records.title: Iatrogenic rectal perforation in two cats secondary to use of a faecal loop.
records.abstract: Two male, neutered, Domestic Shorthair cats, aged 5 and 8 years, were presented to the University of Florida for evaluation and correction of rectal perforations that occurred during faecal sample collection with faecal loops at their primary care hospitals. One cat presented with a fever, neutropenia, and lymphocytosis, while the other had a fever, thrombocytopenia, hyperglycaemia, and was approximately 5% dehydrated. In both cases, radiography identified a heterogeneous soft tissue and gas opacity adjacent to the rectum, and CT scans identified a defect in the rectal wall with associated pocketing, subcutaneous faecal material, and subcutaneous emphysema. The rectal defects were repaired surgically in both cats using a lateral perineal approach. Both surgical sites were treated with open wound management and left to heal by second intention. Iatrogenic rectal perforation. There are risks associated with the use of instruments, such as faecal loops or thermometers, in the rectum. Associated trauma can lead to potentially life-threatening complications. Early detection of rectal perforation is vital to reduce further complications and improve clinical outcomes.

records.title: Exertional syncope caused by acquired obstruction of the pulmonary artery due to an organized thrombus in a dog.
records.abstract: An 8.5-year-old Boxer was referred for evaluation of frequently occurring exercise-induced seizure-like episodes for 2.5 months. Cardiac auscultation revealed a left basilar systolic murmur with an intensity of IV/VI. Echocardiography showed severe pulmonary arterial obstruction with a pressure gradient of 90 mmHg due to a suspected intraluminal mass. Cardiac catheterization was performed, where a right ventriculogram revealed a large rounded filling defect in the pulmonary artery trunk. No balloon angioplasty, biopsy or stenting were attempted. After euthanasia, post-mortem examination revealed an organized thrombus of unknown etiology attached to the wall of the pulmonary artery trunk. The adjacent arterial wall showed a markedly thickened intimal layer. The etiology remains unclear, primarily due to the chronic nature of the condition. Antemortem blood tests and postmortem examination failed to reveal any prothrombotic conditions. Acquired causes of pulmonary arterial obstruction are extremely rare in dogs, and an organized thrombus has not been reported yet.

records.title: Sex steroids in animals absent gonads: A case series.
records.abstract: Identifying possible sources of sex steroids is challenging in animals exhibiting apparent responses in reproductive tissues but presenting with a history of having been neutered. Sex steroids, typically secreted by the gonads, also induce responses in non-reproductive tissues including the skin or brain, sometimes affecting behaviors. The analysis of hormones has become a mainstay of diagnostic endocrinology in small and large animal practice. The repertoire of those with reproductive relevance has expanded significantly with specific immunoassays detecting anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) from either ovarian granulosa or testicular Sertoli cells. This has proven to be extremely useful differentiating neutered animals from those that are not. When AMH is undetectable, indicating neutered status, the possibility of sex steroid secretion by non-gonadal, pathological tissue, or other exogenous sources becomes very real. Reported gonadal status (as stated by owners) is not always reliable given that changes of ownership are common, and neutering is not always complete, complicating initial diagnosis. The cases reported here include several that are unique in either their presentation, diagnostic approach or likely etiologic origin. All were submitted primarily for an assessment of their gonadal status. Collectively, they illustrate, with unusual insight, the utility of AMH as a gonadal biomarker, while obviating the complexity of interpretation of reproductive hormone analyses in supposedly gonadectomized cats, horses and dogs manifesting a variety of apparent, reproductive conditions and pathologies.

records.title: Ecological Implications of Rodenticide Exposure: First Evidence of Bromadiolone Poisoning in an Indian Leopard ( Panthera pardus fusca ).
records.abstract: Large carnivores such as Indian leopard ( Panthera pardus fusca ) play a crucial role in maintaining ecosystem stability. However, they face increasing threats from habitat loss and other anthropogenic pressures. One significant but underreported threat is unintentional or deliberate poisoning, particularly from chemical pesticides. This study reports the first documented case of rodenticide (bromadiolone) poisoning in a large mammalian carnivore in India. In this study, a deceased female leopard (~5 years old) was recovered from the Nilgiris Forest Division, Tamil Nadu, India. Tissues of kidney, liver, and gut contents of the leopard were collected for toxicological investigation. Using high-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), the samples were screened for 51 pesticides. Bromadiolone, a second-generation anticoagulant rodenticide (SGAR), was detected at concentrations of 802.9 ng/g in kidney, 237.7 ng/g in liver, and 39.3 ng/g in gut. No other pesticides were detected in any of the samples studied. Postmortem examination revealed internal hemorrhaging consistent with bromadiolone-induced coagulopathy, confirming it as the likely cause of death. This study underscores the ecological risk posed by rodenticides through deliberate or secondary poisoning of nontarget wildlife. To prevent such incidents, stricter regulations and greater public awareness regarding the use of anticoagulant rodenticides near forested areas are urgently needed. Additionally, long-term monitoring and research on rodenticide exposure are strongly recommended to guide further conservation actions and safeguard wildlife across the country.

records.title: Presumed Leflunomide-Induced Lung Injury in a Dog.
records.journal: Journal of veterinary emergency and critical care (San Antonio, Tex. : 2001)
records.abstract: To describe a clinical case of presumed drug-induced lung disease (DILD) caused by leflunomide, including a clinical case summary and a discussion of current veterinary and translational understandings of the diagnostic and therapeutic approach to DILD and the possible relationship between leflunomide use and interstitial lung disease in a dog. A 1-year-old intact male mixed-breed dog with a history of steroid-responsive meningitis-arteritis managed on prednisone, leflunomide, and cyclosporine was presented for a 2-day history of coughing, vomiting, lethargy, and anorexia. Thoracic radiographs showed an interstitial pulmonary pattern, while computed tomography showed diffuse pulmonary infiltrates and severe tracheobronchial lymphadenomegaly. Diagnostic testing including fungal serology and airway cytology/culture effectively ruled out infectious etiologies. Because the patient responded completely to a cessation of leflunomide therapy and anti-inflammatory doses of corticosteroids, we suspect these signs were the result of DILD as has been reported with leflunomide use in people. This is the first report of leflunomide-induced lung disease in veterinary medicine. Clinicians should be aware of the adverse drug event and use caution when considering this medication in patients with preexisting pulmonary disease.

records.title: Cystic clear cell thymoma in a cat: clinical, imaging, anatomopathological and immunohistochemical findings.
records.abstract: Thymomas are uncommon thymic epithelial neoplasms in cats and may present uncommon histological variants, such as cystic clear cell thymoma. The aim of this case report was to describe the clinical, imaging, anatomopathological, and immunohistochemical findings of a cystic clear cell thymoma in a four-year-old mixed-breed female cat presented with anorexia and progressive dyspnea. Imaging examinations revealed a large heterogeneous mediastinal mass with cystic components, accompanied by pleural effusion and pulmonary compression. Ultrasound-guided cytology was inconclusive. Despite intensive supportive care, the patient died due to respiratory failure. Necropsy revealed a large mediastinal mass occupying approximately 70-80% of the thoracic cavity, accompanied by compressive pulmonary atelectasis and hydrothorax. Histologically, the neoplasm was predominantly composed of carbohydrate-rich clear epithelial cells accompanied by cystic structures, scattered mature lymphocytes and rare Hassall's corpuscles. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated strong nuclear expression of p40, p63 and CKAE1/AE3 in the neoplastic cells, whereas CD3 labeling was restricted to non-neoplastic lymphocytes, supporting the diagnosis of cystic clear cell thymoma. This report expands the current knowledge of this rare tumor variant in cats and highlights the importance of imaging examinations, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry for establishing a definitive diagnosis.

records.title: Description of a transtemporal surgical approach to the mandibular coronoid process region in two dogs with oral pain.
records.journal: The Journal of small animal practice
records.abstract: Conditions affecting the mandibular coronoid process and surgical approaches to it are rarely described in veterinary medicine. We describe and illustrate an alternative surgical approach to the mandibular coronoid process in two dogs. Two dogs presented with a chronic history of pain while opening the mouth. Computed tomography identified unilateral contrast-enhancing soft tissues around the proximal mandibular coronoid process. The mandibular coronoid process in each dog was approached via a transtemporal muscular approach dorsal to the zygomatic arch, without the need for a zygomatic osteotomy. This allowed access to both the proximal medial and lateral aspects of the mandibular coronoid process. A foreign body was surgically identified in one case, whereas no foreign material was retrieved in the other. Both dogs were free of clinical signs up to 6 months postoperatively. The described technique provided a less invasive approach, resulting in reduced tissue damage, reduced postoperative pain and rapid recovery.

records.title: Suspected Incidental Release of Cardiac Tamponade From Chest Compressions in a Dog.
records.journal: Journal of veterinary emergency and critical care (San Antonio, Tex. : 2001)
records.abstract: To describe the clinical presentation, management, and outcome of a dog with suspected pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade that may have been released with chest compressions during CPR. A dog was presented to a primary care veterinarian for dyspnea. Thoracic radiographs showed a globoid cardiac silhouette and no pleural effusion. The dog was transferred immediately to a referral veterinary hospital and was unresponsive and pulseless on arrival. Chest compressions were commenced as part of CPR, and return of spontaneous circulation was achieved. Thoracic radiographs after return of spontaneous circultation showed a more normal-appearing cardiac silhouette and new pleural effusion. An echocardiogram showed a right auricular mass. The dog died at home approximately 48 h after initial presentation. This report describes the first known case of suspected incidental release of cardiac tamponade temporally associated with chest compressions in a dog.

records.title: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Enterobacter hormaechei and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolated from mammary and postoperative wounds in canine oncology patients.
records.abstract: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacterales represent an increasing challenge in small animal medicine due to their limited treatment options and potential for dissemination in clinical settings. Although ESBL-positive Enterobacterales are increasingly recognized in dogs, their detection and clinical significance among dogs with cancer remain poorly investigated. Herein, we report the detection and genomic characterization of three ESBL-producing isolates recovered from wound samples of two dogs with neoplastic diseases. One Enterobacter hormaechei isolate was recovered from an ulcerated mammary tumor, whereas another E. hormaechei isolate and a Klebsiella pneumoniae isolate were recovered from a postoperative wound following thoracic nodulectomy. All three isolates were classified as multidrug-resistant and belonged to clinically relevant sequence types: E. hormaechei sequence type (ST) 114 and ST133, and K. pneumoniae ST11. All isolates carried bla CTX-M-15 , while K. pneumoniae ST11 additionally harbored bla CTX-M-8 . Genomic analyses also identified multiple virulence-associated determinants, including siderophore-associated genes in E. hormaechei ST133. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first published report of E. hormaechei ST133 in a dog. These findings highlight the detection of clinically relevant ESBL-producing lineages in canine oncology patients and reinforce the importance of microbiological surveillance and antimicrobial susceptibility testing in veterinary practice.

records.title: Beating-heart pulmonary arteriotomy under cardiopulmonary bypass for heartworm extraction in three dogs without caval syndrome.
records.abstract: To describe the clinical outcomes of beating-heart open-heart surgery under cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) for surgical extraction of adult heartworms from the pulmonary arteries in dogs without caval syndrome. Animals Three client-owned dogs. Three client-owned dogs with heartworm disease, ≥5 adult heartworms visualized within a single pulmonary arterial branch, and no evidence of caval syndrome were included. After establishment of CPB, the pulmonary artery was opened without cardioplegic arrest, and adult heartworms were surgically extracted. Clinical follow-up ranged from 6 to 22 months, with objective echocardiographic, radiographic, right pulmonary artery distensibility (RPAD) index, and heartworm antigen assessments performed at scheduled follow-up examinations. Study design Case report. Adult heartworms visible intraoperatively were surgically removed in each dog. All dogs survived surgery and were discharged without major perioperative complications. During follow-up, heartworm antigen tests became negative, and no residual heartworms were detected on echocardiographic examinations. Pulmonary arterial dilation and radiographic abnormalities improved, while right pulmonary artery distensibility (RPAD) index values increased from 27.7%, 28.0%, and 22.5% preoperatively to 38.8%, 35.6%, and 35.4%, respectively. Surgical extraction of adult heartworms from the pulmonary arteries was associated with favorable postoperative and follow-up findings in these three dogs.

records.title: Paediatric Lagenidiosis Involving the Lacrimal Sac: A Rare Oomycete Infection in an Immunocompetent Child.
records.abstract: Lagenidium giganteum, an oomycete, causes invasive disease in dogs and horses following freshwater exposure, but only two human infections have been reported, both in adults. We describe a healthy 3-year-old boy who developed a firm lacrimal sac mass over three weeks, following freshwater exposure. Inflammatory markers were normal, and antibacterial therapy was ineffective. Biopsy demonstrated broad, sparsely septate hyphae within granulomatous and eosinophilic inflammation. Routine cultures were initially negative. Prolonged incubation yielded a slow-growing, submerged colony, and internal transcribed spacer sequencing identified Lagenidium giganteum forma caninum. The isolate did not grow sufficiently to facilitate susceptibility testing. Two surgical debridements, performed one week apart, did not achieve complete source control. Twelve months of oral posaconazole and terbinafine with topical natamycin produced sustained clinical and radiologic improvement, maintained after cessation of therapy. This is the first reported paediatric human lagenidiosis and the first involving the lacrimal apparatus.

records.title: Transmural and Intraluminal Gallbladder Hemorrhage (Hemocholecyst) in a Dog Following Snakebite Envenomation.
records.journal: Journal of veterinary emergency and critical care (San Antonio, Tex. : 2001)
records.abstract: To describe a case of hemocholecyst as a sequela to snake envenomation in a dog. A 2-year-old neutered male mixed-breed dog was hospitalized for 4 days after a suspected crotaline envenomation and possible anaphylactic reaction. Significant clinical findings included coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, hyperbilirubinemia, anemia, multiorgan dysfunction, and hypotension. Point-of-care ultrasound was suggestive of gallbladder wall thickening, a finding frequently associated with anaphylaxis or intramural hemorrhage, with other differentials including cholecystitis, mucocele, or neoplasia. Despite aggressive therapy with antivenom, blood products, and supportive care, the dog experienced cardiopulmonary arrest. Necropsy revealed widespread hemorrhage, multiorgan tissue necrosis, pigment nephropathy, and marked obstructive hemorrhage and necrosis of the gallbladder, consistent with hemocholecyst formation. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first report of hemocholecyst as a sequela to snake envenomation in a dog. Obstructive hemocholecyst and transmural gallbladder wall hemorrhage should remain differentials for severe hyperbilirubinemia in dogs with venom-induced coagulopathy.

records.title: Acute Tracheal Narrowing due to Suspected Intramural Tracheal Hemorrhage in a Dog With Hemophilia A.
records.journal: Journal of veterinary emergency and critical care (San Antonio, Tex. : 2001)
records.abstract: To describe a case of spontaneous intramural tracheal hemorrhage with subsequent tracheal narrowing leading to a respiratory crisis in a dog with hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency). A 5-year-old neutered male Havanese presented in respiratory distress following acute-onset cough. The dog had a known history of hemophilia A and had been evaluated at a different facility the day prior, where thoracic radiographs showed severe tracheal attenuation, leading to a presumptive diagnosis of tracheal collapse. The patient was intubated on presentation due to severe respiratory distress. Serial blood work monitoring showed development of anemia and a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time. Intramural tracheal hemorrhage was suspected, and a cryoprecipitate transfusion was administered. Subsequent thoracic radiographs at the 1-week follow-up showed improving tracheal attenuation, with complete resolution of tracheal narrowing. In hindsight, having a high index of suspicion of hemorrhage as the cause of respiratory distress at first presentation, and early transfusion of a factor VIII-containing blood product, would have likely reduced the progression and severity of the clinical episode in this dog. Intramural tracheal hemorrhage can present similarly to tracheal collapse and is a differential for tracheal narrowing on radiographs. There have been previous reports of dogs in respiratory distress with tracheal narrowing due to hemorrhage caused by anticoagulant rodenticide toxicosis. This is the first case report documenting spontaneous hemorrhage secondary to hemophilia A causing tracheal narrowing. Although rare, hemorrhage should be considered in all cases of tracheal narrowing, especially in patients without a chronic history of cough and those that fail to respond to standard treatment for tracheal collapse. Dogs with a known diagnosis of hemophilia A should be assumed to have bleeding almost regardless of their clinical presentation and treated accordingly.

records.title: Gastric ulcers in cats with feline infectious peritonitis.
records.abstract: Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) is one of the leading causes of death in cats worldwide. Although multiple organs can be affected, gastric ulcers have not been previously described as part of the pathological picture. Here we describe the macroscopic, histopathological, and immunohistochemical features of gastric ulcers of four domestic cats with FIP. The mean age of affected cats was 19 months. The affected cats had multisystemic involvement and the disease was classified as three mixed and one non-effusive case of FIP. Gross changes in the stomach were identified in all cases and consisted of single or multiple ulcers of variable diameter that were surrounded by a hyperemic halo. Histologically, ulcerated lesions consisted of areas of mucosal loss with coagulative necrosis surrounded by fibrin and cellular debris and, in some cases, pyogranulomatous inflammation. In the submucosa there was pyogranulomatous vasculitis, thrombosis, and fibrinoid vascular necrosis. All cases had positive immunolabeling for FCoV in the cytoplasm of macrophages within the gastric mucosa and submucosa. Although ulcerative gastritis is not a classic manifestation of FIP, the vasculitis and thrombosis observed in these cases likely contributed to the development of gastric ulcers. FIP should be considered as a differential diagnosis in cats with gastric ulcers associated with pyogranulomatous inflammatory infiltrate.

records.title: Intrametatarsal pad injection of indocyanine green for near-infrared fluorescence imaging of the thoracic duct in four dogs and two cats with chylothorax.
records.abstract: To assess the efficacy of direct near-infrared fluorescence (NIRF) using indocyanine green (ICG) via intrametatarsal pad injection in dogs and cats with idiopathic chylothorax. Retrospective case series of client-owned animals undergoing intrametatarsal ICG injection and thoracoscopic thoracic duct ligation between 2020 and 2025. A total of four dogs and two cats. Inclusion criteria consisted of cytologically confirmed chylothorax, preoperative computed tomography (CT) lymphangiogram (CTL), and known intraoperative injection of ICG in the metatarsal pad(s). Data collected included signalment, weight, preoperative diagnostics, number of ducts visualized intraoperatively, dose of ICG, additional doses required, and concordance with CTL. Time to visualization of the ICG in the thoracic duct, surgical procedures performed, and any intraoperative complications encountered were also reported. Postoperative data included time to discharge, time to first recheck, presence of fluid at first recheck, postoperative complications, status at last recheck, and total follow-up time. Median number of ducts seen between T10 and 13 region on preoperative CT was 2.5 (range: 1-4). The ICG dose ranged from 0.06 to 0.25 mg/kg, and two cases required additional injections to visualize the duct and all branches. A duct not previously seen on CT was visualized with NIRF in one dog. Median time to TD visualization was 7 min (range: 5-22 min). No intra- or postoperative complications due to the metatarsal injections were reported, and all patients were discharged. A total of 5/6 patients did not require thoracocentesis and were clinically well at a median last follow-up of 647 days (range: 454-793). Intrametatarsal injection of ICG appears effective for identification of the thoracic duct in animals with chylothorax.

records.title: Detection of Urinary Round Cells in a Dog With IgA Paraproteinemia: A Case of Myeloma-Related Disorder.
records.abstract: An 11-year-old neutered male Rottweiler mixed-breed dog was presented with apathy, anorexia, and polyuria/polydipsia. Clinicopathologic evaluation revealed hypercalcemia, azotemia, mild hyperproteinemia, and hyperglobulinemia, and proteinuria with concurrent glucosuria. Urinary cytology identified numerous neoplastic round cells morphologically consistent with plasma cells. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated hepatic and splenic hypoechoic lesions, lymphadenomegaly, and hypoechoic prostatic parenchyma. Cytology of aspirates from hepatic and splenic lesions revealed the same neoplastic round cell population as observed in the urine. Based on these findings, a presumptive diagnosis of myeloma-related disorder (MRD), most likely multiple myeloma (MM), was made. Further laboratory investigations were pursued with serum protein electrophoresis (SPE) and immunofixation (IM), as well as immunocytochemistry. SPE coupled with IM revealed an IgA paraproteinemia, and immunocytochemistry findings were suggestive of plasma cell differentiation. The present findings are indicative of an MRD. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first description of plasmacytoid cells in urine from a dog with concurrent paraproteinemia, highlighting urine cytology as a potential non-invasive diagnostic tool for MRD.

records.title: A rare case of disseminated mucocutaneous candidiasis in a dog.
records.abstract: A 6-year-old, neutered, male, mongrel dog was referred to the oncology team with numerous ulcerated nodules distributed throughout the skin and mucocutaneous regions. With the initial suspicion of a recurrent canine transmissible venereal tumor, fine-needle aspiration cytology was performed on a 5 × 4 cm ulcerated nodule in the ventral abdomen; however, the findings were similar to reactive cutaneous histiocytosis. The dog was then referred for biopsy and histopathological examination, which confirmed chronic pyogranulomatous dermatitis with intralesional fungal structures. Culture enabled a conclusive diagnosis of a rare case of disseminated mucocutaneous candidiasis (DMC). Treatment with itraconazole was administered, with complete clinical remission achieved within two months, demonstrating the importance of appropriate diagnosis and therapy.

records.title: Electrochemotherapy for urinary bladder botryoid rhabdomyosarcoma in a dog: case report.
records.abstract: Urinary bladder rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is a rare malignant neoplasm in dogs, most commonly affecting young animals and frequently arising from the trigone region, where complete surgical removal is challenging. Reported median survival time for dogs with vesical RMS is 45 days, ranging from 20 to 120 days. This report describes the diagnosis and multimodal treatment of a six-month-old intact female Golden Retriever diagnosed with vesical botryoid rhabdomyosarcoma. The patient presented with urinary incontinence, dysuria, and hematuria and was initially treated for suspected cystitis without clinical improvement. Ultrasonography identified a bladder mass located in the trigone region, and exploratory cystotomy with surgical debulking was performed. Intraoperative electrochemotherapy with bleomycin was administered, followed by six sessions of systemic doxorubicin chemotherapy. Complete remission was achieved, but recurrence was noted after 183 days, and the patient presented a survival time of 277 days, exceeding previously reported outcomes for this neoplasm. Although disease progression ultimately occurred, this case suggests that incorporating electrochemotherapy into a multimodal protocol may improve locoregional control in infiltrative vesical rhabdomyosarcoma and potentially prolong survival in dogs affected by this malignancy.

records.title: Laparoscopic-assisted treatment of giant urachal cyst in a female Dachshund.
records.abstract: To describe the clinical features and successful surgical management of a giant, symptomatic urachal cyst (UC) in a dog using a laparoscopic-assisted approach without partial cystectomy. Computed tomography (CT) and cystography identified a 13-cm cystic lesion at the bladder apex without luminal communication. A laparoscopic exploration was initially attempted either for cyst resection, or for decortication combined with omentalization. Following percutaneous aspiration of the cyst, the lesion was dissected from the surrounding omental adhesion. Due to the inability to identify the course of both ureters and the indistinct anatomical margins between the cyst and the bladder, the procedure was converted to a mini-laparotomy. The cystic wall was readily separated from the bladder apex by blunt dissection and completely excised after circumferential incision at the external junction between the cyst and the bladder using a vessel sealing device. Following omentalization of the cyst resection site, the bladder was returned to its anatomical position within the peritoneal cavity. Postoperative recovery was uneventful. Transient apical bulging and discomfort during bladder distension were observed on postoperative cystography, attributed to a localized compliance mismatch between the denuded bladder wall and the stiffer, thermally coagulated region. Bladder capacity normalized by day 21 with a normal bladder silhouette. Histopathology confirmed a subserosal UC with no evidence of malignancy. The patient remained clinically well, and no recurrence was noted during a 20-month follow-up. Laparoscopic-assisted resection was an effective, minimally invasive treatment for the giant UC in this dog. Consistent with current human medical guidelines, simple marginal excision without partial cystectomy proved feasible and sufficient for a UC lacking luminal communication, regardless of lesion size.

records.title: Squamous cell carcinoma involving the anal sac region in a cat: clinical course and multimodal management with toceranib and electrochemotherapy.
records.abstract: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is one of the most common malignant epithelial tumours in cats, typically arising in the oral cavity or at cutaneous sites, whereas involvement of the anal sac region is exceptionally rare, with only two cases previously reported. An 8-year-old neutered male Domestic Shorthair cat was referred for persistent tenesmus, constipation and anorexia. A perianal swelling had initially been interpreted as anal sacculitis on cytology, but incisional biopsies confirmed SCC, characterised histologically by only moderate atypia and a low mitotic count. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a non-circumferential mass centred on the left anal sac region with infiltration of the perirectal soft tissues causing partial rectal obstruction, together with regional lymphadenomegaly; nodal metastasis was confirmed cytologically. Surgery and radiation therapy were declined, and palliative treatment with toceranib phosphate and meloxicam was started. After approximately one month of clinically stable disease, one session of electrochemotherapy with intravenous bleomycin was performed. Clinical signs transiently improved, but rapid progression occurred shortly thereafter, with invasion of the pelvic urethra. The cat died 68 days after diagnosis. Despite reassuring histological features, the tumour showed aggressive local behaviour and early regional metastasis. Toceranib was associated with transient clinical improvement and electrochemotherapy produced only short-lived improvement, likely because the lesion's extent and depth precluded complete treatment of the tumour volume. records.title: Genomic analysis of extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolated from a dog with a severe episode of self-trauma and urinary tract infection.
records.abstract: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacterales are emerging pathogens of major importance in veterinary medicine. records.title: Multiple cartilaginous exostosis in a feline: Case report.
records.abstract: Multiple cartilaginous exostoses (MCE), or osteochondromatosis, is a benign neoplasm characterized by the presence of nodules on the bone surface. records.abstract: To describe the clinical presentation, diagnosis, and management of hypocalcemia secondary to inadvertent administration of denosumab in a 4-month-old kitten. A 4-month-old neutered female domestic shorthair kitten was presented with acute weakness, tremors, third eyelid prolapse, and ataxia for several hours. Physical examination revealed lethargy, tachycardia, hypothermia, mild dehydration, and apparent nausea. Neurologic findings included tremors, cerebellar ataxia, bilateral mydriasis, and decreased bilateral direct and indirect pupillary reflexes. ECG confirmed sinus tachycardia. Blood work showed severe ionized hypocalcemia (0.74 mmol/L [2.96 mg/dL]; reference interval [RI]: 1.10-1.40 [4.40-5.60]), mild hypokalemia (3.38 mmol/L [3.38 mEq/L]; RI: 3.90-4.90 [3.90-4.90]), and moderate hyperglycemia (10.8 mmol/L [194 mg/dL]; RI: 3.6-6.2 [64.86-111.71]). The owner later disclosed an accidental subcutaneous injection to the kitten with denosumab 1 week earlier, strongly suggesting drug-induced hypocalcemia. Treatment with IV calcium gluconate 10% (0.5 mL/kg over 10 min twice) resolved signs and normalized iCa (1.20 mmol/L [4.8 mg/dL]). Isotonic crystalloids with potassium and maropitant were given for hydration, electrolyte correction, and nausea. Oral calcium (60 mg/kg, q 24 h) was started on Day 1; iCa remained normal (1.26 mmol/L [5.04 mg/dL]) at Day 2, and the kitten was discharged. At Day 11, iCa was 1.19 mmol/L [4.76 mg/dL], the dose was halved, and at Day 18, iCa remained normal (1.24 mmol/L [4.96 mg/dL]), allowing for discontinuation of therapy. The clinical manifestations and diagnosis are described, along with the details of management that led to the kitten in this report making a full recovery.

records.title: More than a scratch, Capnocytophaga bacteremia induced severe sepsis with multi-organ failure with occupational dog exposure: A case report.
records.abstract: Capnocytophaga  species are fastidious gram-negative bacilli found in the oral flora of dogs and cats. Although human infection is typically associated with localized soft tissue disease following animal exposure, invasive infection can result in severe sepsis. We present a case of  Capnocytophaga  bacteremia in an immunocompetent woman with occupational exposure to dogs. A 49-year-old woman with a history of Factor V Leiden mutation, prior deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, and Raynaud's syndrome presented with fever, chills, fatigue, myalgias, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and transient vaginal bleeding. Evaluation revealed acute kidney injury, lactic acidosis, transaminitis, severe thrombocytopenia, and a petechial rash. An extensive infectious and autoimmune workup was unrevealing. Further history revealed recurrent occupational exposure to dogs as a photographer and walker, including a recent healing scratch to her right arm without evidence of local infection. Due to persistent leukocytosis and lack of clinical improvement, antimicrobial therapy was escalated to meropenem, resulting in gradual clinical and laboratory recovery. Blood cultures eventually grew  Capnocytophaga  species after delayed growth on anaerobic media. The patient was transitioned to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate to complete a two-week course. Susceptibility testing could not be performed because of insufficient organism growth. This case highlights the potential for severe  Capnocytophaga  bacteremia in an immunocompetent host with recurrent occupational exposure to animals. The nonspecific presentation and difficulty identifying this fastidious organism contributed to diagnostic uncertainty and delayed targeted therapy. Clinicians should consider  Capnocytophaga  infection in patients with unexplained sepsis and a history of animal exposure, even in the absence of a significant bite wound or overt soft-tissue infection.

records.title: Ovarian leiomyoma with an epithelioid differentiation in a dog.
records.journal: The Journal of veterinary medical science
records.abstract: A 12-years-3-months-old female Toy Poodle underwent ovariohysterectomy, and an 8-mm ovarian mass was incidentally identified on pathological examination. Histopathologically, the oval area was composed of interlacing fascicles of spindle neoplastic cells with elongated to cigar-shaped nuclei, whereas the crescent-shaped peripheral area contained solitary or clustered polygonal to round neoplastic cells scattered within myxoid stroma. Cytokeratin expression was observed in the polygonal to round neoplastic cells, but not in the spindle neoplastic cells. Collectively, the tumor was diagnosed as an ovarian leiomyoma with an epithelioid differentiation.

records.title: Histological and proteomic characterization of hyaline material in two dogs with hyalinizing pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
records.journal: The Journal of veterinary medical science
records.abstract: Hyalinizing pancreatic adenocarcinoma is a rare subtype of exocrine pancreatic carcinoma in dogs, characterized by abundant extracellular hyaline material within the tumor. In this study, we investigated two canine cases exhibiting this distinctive hyalinizing morphology using histological, proteomic, immunohistochemical, ultrastructural, and molecular approaches. Histological examination revealed amyloid-like eosinophilic hyaline deposits; however, these deposits lacked diagnostic features of amyloid, as confirmed by Congo red and thioflavin S staining and transmission electron microscopy. Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) identified bile salt-activated lipase (BAL) as the predominant component of the hyaline deposits. Immunohistochemistry confirmed strong anti-BAL immunoreactivity in the deposits. In addition to BAL, amyloid-associated proteins, including clusterin, vitronectin, apolipoprotein E, and apolipoprotein A-I, were detected. Together with the negative Congo red and thioflavin S staining and ultrastructural findings, these results support that the hyaline deposits are BAL-rich, non-amyloid extracellular deposits. Some deposits also contained collagen, indicating biochemical heterogeneity of the hyaline material. RT-qPCR analysis suggested higher CEL, and lower GRP94 expression in hyalinizing pancreatic adenocarcinomas than in non-hyalinizing pancreatic carcinomas. These observations raise a hypothesis that excessive BAL production, together with reduced GRP94-mediated chaperone support, may contribute to extracellular accumulation of aggregated BAL. Collectively, this study identifies BAL as the predominant component of hyaline deposits in canine hyalinizing pancreatic adenocarcinoma based on LC-MS/MS analysis and highlights a non-amyloid protein aggregation process associated with this tumor subtype.

records.title: A dog with suspected hypothalamic hypoadrenocorticism classified by corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) testing.
records.journal: The Journal of veterinary medical science
records.abstract: A 7-year-old intact male toy poodle presented with abdominal distension, polydipsia, and polyuria. To localize dysfunction within the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, a corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) stimulation test was performed. Endogenous ACTH increased markedly after CRH administration, whereas cortisol remained undetectable, demonstrating preserved pituitary responsiveness and supporting a diagnosis of hypothalamic hypoadrenocorticism. Treatment of hypoadrenocorticism with prednisolone alone resulted in long-term clinical stabilization without electrolyte abnormalities for over one year. To our knowledge, this is the first canine report classifying suspected hypothalamic hypoadrenocorticism using CRH stimulation testing.

records.title: Esophageal strictures associated with prolonged nasoesophageal tube placement in three cats.
records.abstract: Nasoesophageal tube placement for a prolonged period of time has not previously been associated with esophageal stricture in cats. Three cats with suspected hepatic lipidosis required extended enteral nutritional support because voluntary food intake remained < 25% of the calculated resting energy requirement. Regurgitation or retching developed within 1-3 days after tube removal, and esophagoscopy identified severe focal strictures in the cervical esophagus at the C4-C6 vertebral level in all 3 cats. One cat underwent 3 endoscopic balloon dilatation sessions at 1-week intervals, with enlargement of the esophageal lumen. The consistent anatomic location and temporal association with prolonged tube placement suggest that extended nasoesophageal intubation may be a risk factor for cervical esophageal stricture formation in cats. When prolonged nutritional support is anticipated, transition to a feeding tube intended for long-term use should be considered.

records.abstract: Multicentric lymphoma is one of the most common haematopoietic neoplasms in dogs and may present with variable systemic and cardiothoracic manifestations. records.abstract: Pork-cat syndrome (PCS) is caused by cross-reactivity between cat serum albumin (Fel d 2) and pork serum albumin (Sus s 1). We report an 11-year-old boy with food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis (FDEIA) in whom milk was identified as the trigger and serum albumin cross-reactivity was suspected as a possible mechanism. Skin prick testing was positive for raw pork, raw beef, pork sausage, and unheated milk, but negative for heated pork, heated beef, and heated milk. In an oral food challenge, symptoms were reproduced after exercise following ingestion of 300 mL of unheated milk, leading to a diagnosis of milk-related FDEIA. Inhibition enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay demonstrated partial inhibition of IgE reactivity to Bos d 6 by pork, cat hair, and milk extracts at the tested concentration. These findings suggested serum albumin cross-reactivity involving PCS. This case highlights the clinical utility of component-resolved diagnosis, particularly low casein-specific IgE with high Bos d 6-specific IgE, in raising suspicion of serum albumin-related mechanisms in patients with milk-related FDEIA.

records.title: Adjuvant Interstitial Yttrium-90 Hydrogel (IsoPet ® ) Following Limb-Sparing Marginal Excision of Multifocal Distal Pelvic-Limb Neoplasia in a Dog.
records.journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
records.abstract: Achieving complete surgical margins can be challenging for tumors involving the distal extremities due to limited surrounding soft tissue and the proximity of functionally important structures. Incompletely excised tumors may require adjuvant radiation therapy to treat suspected residual microscopic disease. Yttrium-90 phosphate hydrogel (IsoPet ® ) is an emerging injectable radiation modality that delivers localized beta radiation to a tumor bed or surgical margin. An eight-year-old neutered male Bullmastiff was evaluated by the referring veterinarian for firm subcutaneous masses developed along the right pelvic limb. Fine-needle aspiration was initially suggestive of an inflammatory process; however, subsequent punch biopsies identified Grade II soft tissue sarcoma. The patient was referred for surgical oncology evaluation. Four right pelvic limb masses and the right popliteal lymph node were surgically excised. Histopathological examination of the excisional specimens identified poorly differentiated carcinoma involving the excised masses, with metastatic involvement of the right popliteal lymph node and incomplete surgical margins. Adjuvant Y-90 hydrogel was elected following complete surgical wound healing. On 20 November 2025, 8.46 mCi (313 MBq) of Y-90 phosphate hydrogel in a total volume of 4.7 mL was administered through 66 peri-incisional and incisional injections distributed across the previous right pelvic limb surgical beds using a grid-based technique. The procedure was completed without complications. Post-treatment follow-up demonstrated satisfactory wound healing, with only mild transient appetite reduction and minimal localized tissue irritation. After surgery plus adjuvant Y-90, no clinically detectable local recurrence was identified at the treatment sites during the 120-day documented follow-up period. records.title: Acute Levothyroxine Overdose Followed by Serial Monitoring of Total Thyroxine and Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone in a Hypothyroid Dog.
records.abstract: Reports of acute levothyroxine overdose in dogs are rare with limited monitoring data. An 8-year-old spayed female Pomeranian receiving long-term hypothyroidism treatment presented 9 h after ingesting a one-month supply of levothyroxine (3 mg; 1.13 mg/kg). Except for transient tachycardia, the physical examination revealed unremarkable findings. The total thyroxine (T4) level exceeded the upper limit of quantification. Levothyroxine was discontinued, and activated charcoal and intravenous fluid were administered. The dog showed normal vital signs and no further clinical abnormalities during the 5-day hospitalisation. The total T4 concentration decreased and normalised by 73 h after the overdose. The canine thyroid-stimulating hormone (cTSH) concentrations were initially normal but exceeded the upper reference limit at 98 h. The patient was discharged on Day 5. Two days later, levothyroxine was resumed because the dog exhibited signs of recurrent hypothyroidism with persistently elevated cTSH levels. Hypothyroidism was well-controlled for 6 months. To our knowledge, this is the first report to document a levothyroxine overdose in a hypothyroid dog using daily total T4 and cTSH monitoring. These findings suggest that acute overdose is less severe than chronic levothyroxine exposure.

records.title: Chronic Recurrent Septic Peritonitis in a Diabetic Dog Caused by Staphylococcus pseudintermedius With Splendore-Hoeppli Reaction (Botryomycosis-Like/Bacterial Pseudomycetoma).

records.title: Chemodectoma Arising From the Abdominal Aorta in a 9-Year-Old Female Dog: Clinical, Histopathological and Immunohistochemstric Study.
records.abstract: Chemodectomas are uncommon, typically benign neoplasms derived from paraganglionic chemoreceptor tissues, most frequently arising in the heart base or carotid bodies of brachycephalic dogs. This report documents a detailed pathological description of a chemodectoma originating from the abdominal aorta in a non-human species, representing, to our knowledge, the first case specifically characterized by its origin at the aortic trifurcation, thereby expanding the recognized anatomical spectrum of this tumour entity. A 9-year-old spayed female terrier was presented with persistent panting, recent-onset obesity following previous cachexia, and a complex clinical history including polyuria/polydipsia and pyoderma. Haematological and biochemical analyses revealed a regenerative anaemia, leucocytosis, and biochemical indicators suggestive of cholestasis and potential endocrinopathy. Advanced imaging identified a solitary, well-demarcated, highly vascular abdominal mass closely associated with the aortic trifurcation. Given the tumour's inaccessibility and pronounced vascularity, cytological confirmation via fine needle aspiration was precluded due to haemorrhagic risk, necessitating exploratory laparotomy. Intraoperatively, the mass was unresectable because of its anatomical relationships and the prohibitive risk of catastrophic haemorrhage. Humane euthanasia was subsequently elected. Histopathological evaluation demonstrated a lobulated neoplasm composed of pleomorphic neuroendocrine cells, with low mitotic activity and an absence of necrosis or haemorrhage. Immunohistochemistry confirmed strong, diffuse synaptophysin reactivity and focal neuron-specific enolase positivity, while chromogranin A and S100 protein were negative, underscoring immunophenotypic variability. This case illustrates the diagnostic complexity and therapeutic limitations posed by extra-cardiac chemodectomas in veterinary species, especially when located in unconventional anatomical sites. Limitations included the unavailability of computed tomography and lack of postoperative follow-up. This report expands the recognized clinico-pathological spectrum of chemodectomas and highlights the necessity for multidisciplinary diagnostic strategies and further research aimed at defining optimal management protocols for such rare and challenging presentations.

records.title: Primary Erythrocytosis (Polycythaemia) in a Neutered Male Dog Presenting With Right Hindlimb Lameness.
records.abstract: A 2-year-old male entire Cocker Spaniel was referred for investigation of progressive right hindlimb lameness and polyuria and polydipsia. Neurological examination only revealed a mild short-strided gait, and orthopaedic examination was unremarkable. Initial management involved repeated phlebotomies, followed by long-term treatment with hydroxyurea (31 mg/kg twice weekly) and rivaroxaban (2 mg/kg once daily). At the 5-month recheck, the dog was asymptomatic, with resolution of the iliac thrombus and a normal haematocrit. This case highlights an unusual presentation of PE in a dog, not previously described in the veterinary literature, and re-examines the discussion on the optimal management of this rare condition, with a focus on the necessity of antithrombotic therapy.

records.title: Unilateral Hormonally Active Testicular Sertoli Cell Tumour and Feminization Syndrome in a Bernese Mountain Dog With Normally Descended Testes.

records.title: Intraoperative Indocyanine Green Fluorescence for Assessment of Suspected Venous Invasion in a Dog With Thyroid Carcinoma.
records.abstract: Accurate intraoperative assessment of vascular involvement in canine thyroid carcinoma remains challenging when preoperative imaging findings are equivocal. This case describes the use of intraoperative indocyanine green fluorescence imaging to assist real-time assessment of suspected venous involvement during canine thyroidectomy. A 5-year-old spayed female Maltese dog was presented with a cervical mass and clinicopathological findings consistent with hypothyroidism. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography identified a left thyroid mass with suspected external jugular vein compression but no definitive evidence of vascular invasion. During left thyroidectomy, dilation and distal tapering of the thyroid veins raised concern for venous involvement. Indocyanine green (0.5 mg/dog) was administered intravenously for intraoperative near-infrared fluorescence imaging. Diffuse fluorescence of the thyroid mass and segmental intraluminal fluorescence within the dilated thyroid vein were observed, with signal loss at the tapering point. Based on these findings, en bloc resection including a short segment of the involved vein was performed. Histopathology confirmed thyroid carcinoma without evidence of regional lymph node metastasis. This case illustrates that intraoperative indocyanine green fluorescence imaging may provide adjunctive real-time information for assessing suspected venous involvement during canine thyroid carcinoma surgery and may complement preoperative imaging when vascular invasion is uncertain.

records.title: Carotid body carcinoma in a French bulldog treated with toceranib phosphate.
records.journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
records.abstract: Carotid body tumors are rare neuroendocrine neoplasms in dogs, and evidence-based treatment options for malignant or unresectable cases remain poorly defined. On a later follow-up  via  telephone, the owner reported that the dog had died 6 mo after initiation of targeted therapy. records.title: Clinical and  18 F-FDG PET/CT imaging features in a dog with bacterial sepsis of unknown origin.
records.journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
records.abstract: Positron emission tomography with 2-deoxy-2-[fluorine-18] fluoro-D-glucose integrated with computed tomography ( 18 F-FDG PET/CT) imaging identified infection and inflammation earlier and with higher sensitivity than other imaging modalities in human medicine. A small case series explored the use of  18 F-FDG PET/CT for detecting the cause of fever of unknown origin in dogs. This report details clinical aspects and  18 F-FDG PET/CT imaging in the workup and treatment of a 12-year-old dog that was presented obtunded with severe neutropenia and hypoglycemia secondary to suspected sepsis. The  18 F-FDG PET/CT revealed moderate, patchy FDG avidity and soft-tissue swelling of the left carpus and tarsus (SUV max: 7.18 and SUV max: 5.58, respectively), moderate heterogeneous splenic and hepatic hypermetabolic activity (SUV max: 3.42), and bilaterally symmetric renal hypermetabolic activity (SUV max: 6.22) without appropriate flourine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose ( 18 F-FDG) excretion. Other notable findings included marked, diffuse  18 F-FDG uptake within all bone marrow spaces (SUV max: 15.47) and a generalized, mild lymphadenopathy with moderate hypermetabolic activity. Positive blood cultures confirmed sepsis. Clinical deterioration despite appropriate antibiotic and supportive therapy prompted euthanasia. Necropsy revealed lymphohistiocytic and neutrophilic necrotizing vasculitis with thrombosis and necrosis in heart, spleen, brain, and liver, consistent with septicemia.  Enterococcus faecium  was isolated from lungs, kidneys, and spleen;  Serratia marcescens  was isolated from lungs and kidneys. This is the first documented report of the use of  18 F-FDG PET/CT for the diagnostic workup of a septic patient in veterinary medicine with corroborative necropsy findings to confirm PET/CT suspicion of disseminated septicemia. Key clinical message: Positron emission tomography with 2-deoxy-2-[fluorine-18] fluoro-D-glucose integrated with computed tomography imaging, which combines the functional, metabolic information from a PET scan with the high-resolution anatomical detail from a CT scan, should be considered as an adjunctive imaging modality for the diagnostic workup to identify focal and systemic infections in veterinary medicine. This is critical for immunocompromised animals in which timely and accurate diagnosis is of utmost importance, either for guiding case management and clinical outcome or for guiding owners through difficult decisions when the prognosis is guarded to poor.

records.title: Ultrasonographic features and clinical outcome of an anaplastic carcinoma arising from a uterus masculinus in an intact, non-cryptorchid male dog.
records.journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
records.abstract: A 6-year-old intact male dog was referred because of persistent hematuria despite multiple courses of antimicrobial therapy. Urogenital ultrasonography revealed a large, paraprostatic, uterus-like, fluid-filled structure containing echogenic fluid, associated with an adjacent large, heterogeneous mass located cranially and to the right of the lesion. These findings raised suspicion for malignant transformation of a uterus masculinus associated with persistent Müllerian duct syndrome. Exploratory laparotomy confirmed the presence of a uterus masculinus with blind-ended uterine horns, associated adhesions, and a large mass arising from the right cranial aspect. Surgical excision of the abnormal structure and orchiectomy were carried out. Histopathology confirmed an anaplastic carcinoma of Müllerian origin arising from persistent Müllerian duct remnants. The tumor exhibited highly aggressive biological behavior characterized by extensive local invasion. There was rapid clinical deterioration after surgery, including imaging findings consistent with pulmonary, hepatic, and peritoneal metastatic disease, ultimately leading to euthanasia 5 wk after diagnosis. Key clinical message: Persistent Müllerian duct remnants should be considered as a differential diagnosis for paraprostatic cavitary lesions in intact male dogs, even in the absence of cryptorchidism. Malignant transformation of a uterus masculinus, though rare, may exhibit highly aggressive biological behavior with rapid metastatic dissemination.

records.title: Treatment of Refractory Vomiting With Traditional Chinese Veterinary Medicine in Two Dogs and a Cat: A Cases Series.
records.abstract: Refractory vomiting in dogs and cats is a common clinical condition in small animal practice, typically characterized by recurrent vomiting, belching and related symptoms, which is a great challenge to veterinarians. According to Traditional Chinese Veterinary Medicine (TCVM), this condition is primarily attributed to dysfunction of the spleen and stomach in transformation and transportation, leading to the upward rebellion of stomach Qi. Derived from the Shang Han Lun (Treatise on Cold Damage), Xuanfu Daizhe Decoction functions to direct rebellious Qi downward, resolve phlegm, tonify Qi and harmonize the stomach. It is mainly indicated for conditions resulting from stomach Qi counter flow. In this report, three cases of refractory vomiting in two dogs and a cat diagnosed as stomach Qi rebellion according to TCVM were treated with modified Xuanfu Daizhe Decoction based on syndrome differentiation. The results showed that all three cases achieved favourable therapeutic outcomes. These findings suggest that, for refractory vomiting caused by stomach Qi rebellion in dogs and cats, individualized treatment with modified Xuanfu Daizhe Decoction based on specific clinical presentations can achieve stable and reliable efficacy.

records.title: Novel Therapy for Severe Bilateral Pyogranulomatous Blepharitis Secondary to Hyaluronic Acid Filler in a Dog.
records.abstract: A 9-year-old female spayed mixed breed dog was initially examined for severe bilateral entropion secondary to enophthalmos from chronic oral steroid use for immune-mediated thrombocytopenia as well as potential historic masticatory muscle myositis. records.title: Removal of a lodged endotracheal tube in an anaesthetised French Bulldog using manual laryngeal stabilisation and neuromuscular blockade, and subsequent complications.
records.abstract: A 5-year-old, female neutered French Bulldog presented under anaesthesia with an endotracheal tube (ETT) lodged in the larynx. records.title: Rare Feline Gingival Extramedullary Plasmacytoma: Clinical Application of Electrochemotherapy for Local Control.
records.abstract: Feline extramedullary plasmacytoma (EMP) is an uncommon plasma cell neoplasm typically regarded as biologically benign; however, its clinical behaviour may be heterogeneous. As complete surgical excision was declined, and tumour regrowth occurred after repeated radiation therapy, electrochemotherapy (ECT) was selected for local tumour control. Bleomycin (15,000 IU/m 2  IV) was administered before pulse delivery, and three ECT sessions were performed at weekly intervals. The tumour volume decreased by more than 70%, which was consistent with a partial response, and only mild self-limiting local adverse effects were observed. No systemic toxicity was observed. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report describing the use of ECT for feline gingival EMP. This case highlights the potential biological heterogeneity of feline EMP and suggests that ECT may provide short-term local tumour reduction and palliation when complete surgical excision is not feasible.

records.title: Spontaneous Reduction in Mitral Valve Regurgitation in Three Dogs With Severe Myxomatous Mitral Valve Disease: An Unusual Case Report.
records.abstract: Myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD), the most common heart disease in small-breed dogs, is characterized by mitral regurgitation (MR) resulting from valvular degeneration, which may progress to left-sided heart failure. Standard treatment, including diuretics, improved their conditions; however, further monitoring revealed that the coaptation gap decreased due to mitral valve thickening, leading to a reduction in MR. This was accompanied by a significant decrease in heart size. As a result, diuretics were discontinued, and all dogs were successfully managed with pimobendan alone. To our knowledge, this is the first report of spontaneous MR reduction in MMVD, where coaptation gap narrowing played a role in clinical improvement. These cases may broaden the current understanding of MMVD progression, suggesting that, in rare instances, changes in cardiac remodelling and clinical status can occur. Further research is warranted to better understand the underlying mechanisms.

records.title: Left Medial Liver Lobe Torsion Associated With Hepatocellular Carcinoma in a Pembroke Welsh Corgi: A Case Report.
records.abstract: Liver lobe torsion (LLT) is a rare, potentially life-threatening condition in dogs and is reported most often in medium- to large-breed dogs. The dog recovered uneventfully, was discharged on postoperative Day 4 and had no recurrence of clinical abnormalities at 1-year follow-up. records.title: Anterior Segment OCT Diagnosis of Descemet's Membrane Detachment in a Cat With Suspected FIP-Associated Uveitis.
records.abstract: Persistent corneal edema in cats with anterior uveitis is often attributed to endothelial dysfunction; however, the underlying structural cause may not be apparent without advanced imaging. Descemet's membrane detachment (DMD) is rarely reported in cats and has not been well described in suspected feline infectious peritonitis (FIP)-associated uveitis. A 4-month-old intact male Norwegian Forest cat presented with severe unilateral granulomatous uveitis, mutton-fat keratic precipitates, diffuse stromal edema, and a 2+ aqueous flare. Aqueous humor PCR detected feline coronavirus RNA, although biotype testing did not confirm a mutation consistent with that associated with feline infectious peritonitis virus. As ocular inflammation progressed despite anti-inflammatory treatment, the nucleoside analog GS-441524 was administered along with anti-inflammatory and supportive ophthalmic treatment. Intraocular inflammation improved, but corneal edema persisted, prompting anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT), which revealed planar DMD. Serial AS-OCT monitored posterior corneal structural changes. Corneal edema gradually decreased, and Descemet's membrane reapposition was documented by AS-OCT approximately one year after the initial presentation. Corneal clarity and stability were maintained without clinically evident recurrence for 18 months after reapposition was confirmed. This case describes the AS-OCT diagnosis and serial documentation of DMD and subsequent Descemet's membrane reapposition in a cat with suspected FIP-associated uveitis. These findings highlight the value of AS-OCT for identifying and monitoring posterior corneal abnormalities, including DMD, in cats with severe anterior uveitis and persistent corneal edema. The relationships among suspected FIP-associated uveitis, treatment, and DMD could not be determined from this single case.

records.title: Meibomian Gland Epithelioma Mimicking Eyelid Squamous Cell Carcinoma in a Hereford-Cross Steer.
records.abstract: To describe the clinical presentation and histopathology of a meibomian gland epithelioma that clinically resembled squamous cell carcinoma in a steer. A 15 year-old Hereford-Lowline cross steer presented for evaluation of an approximately 2 × 4 cm ulcerated, pedunculated eyelid mass arising from the right inferior eyelid margin. Excision of the mass followed by adjunctive cryotherapy was performed. The mass was submitted for histopathologic analysis. Histopathologic evaluation revealed the mass to be consistent with a meibomian gland epithelioma, a neoplastic proliferation of the basal/reserve cells of the meibomian gland. The steer recovered routinely from the procedure with no evidence of regrowth of the mass at 13 months post-operatively. Meibomian gland epitheliomas are one of the most common eyelid tumors of dogs; however, this is the first known report of a histologically confirmed meibomian gland epithelioma in cattle. Clinically, the mass resembled the appearance of squamous cell carcinoma, a common eyelid tumor in Hereford cattle. The clinical misclassification of a benign eyelid mass as squamous cell carcinoma could lead to unnecessary aggressive management such as enucleation, exenteration, or culling. This case confirms the importance of histopathologic analysis of excised tissues to reach an accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment and follow-up plans.

records.title: Computed Tomographic Findings of Ischemic Necrosis of the Accessory Carpal Bone in a Dog.
records.journal: Veterinary radiology & ultrasound : the official journal of the American College of Veterinary Radiology and the International Veterinary Radiology Association
records.abstract: A 1-year-and-9-month-old Golden Retriever presented with a 9-month history of right thoracic limb lameness. Radiographs revealed a monostotic, expansile lesion of the right accessory carpal bone (ACB). A computed tomography (CT) confirmed the aggressive nature of the lesion, demonstrating multifocal moth-eaten osteolysis, sclerosis, periosteal reaction, and flexor carpi ulnaris tendinopathy. Differential diagnoses included the ischemic necrosis of the ACB, osteomyelitis, and primary bone neoplasia. Histopathology confirmed osteonecrosis. This case highlights the value of CT in evaluating aggressive carpal lesions and identifies ischemic necrosis as an important differential diagnosis. This case represents the first CT description of this disease in dogs.

records.title: Idiopathic Granulomatous Inflammation of the Periocular Structures in Four Dogs: Clinical, Histopathological, and Imaging Findings and Therapeutic Outcome.
records.abstract: To describe cases of canine idiopathic periocular granulomatous inflammation. Clinical records were reviewed. At the time of presentation, the four patients (German Shepherd dog, mixed breed, Magyar Vizsla, Hovawart) were 1.5-5 (mean 3.75) years old. All dogs were female; two were spayed. Lesions were unilateral in 3/4 cases. Dogs presented with ulcerated (1) or non-ulcerated (3) mass lesions affecting the periocular skin (3/4), medial canthal area (2/4), or third eyelid (1/4). Incisional biopsies revealed pyogranulomatous inflammation in three and granulomatous inflammation in one case. There was no evidence of microbial infection in the specimens. Patients received anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive dosages of systemic corticosteroids. Three dogs also received systemic cyclosporin (5 mg/kg, sid), and one dog received topical cyclosporin (0.1%, bid). One dog underwent surgical debulking of a circumscribed mass within the left lower eyelid prior to immunosuppressive therapy and developed an additional swelling on the left upper eyelid. Remission of clinical signs was achieved in all patients. Dogs were treated for 5 to 11 months (mean 8.7). No recurrence was reported in 4/4 patients during a mean follow-up period of 17.3 months. In 3/4patients, there was no recurrence within an average of 11 months after discontinuation of therapy. One dog was lost to follow-up. Idiopathic granulomatous inflammation is a differential diagnosis for periocular mass lesions. Its diagnosis is based on histopathology and the exclusion of other causes of granulomatous inflammation.

records.title: Staged caval occlusion enabling en bloc right divisional hepatectomy in two dogs with hepatocellular carcinoma.
records.abstract: To describe staged pre-renal caudal vena cava (CVC) occlusion before en bloc right divisional hepatectomy with segmental caval resection in two dogs with right divisional hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) involving the CVC. Two client-owned, 11-year-old neutered male dogs (Siberian Husky and Shih Tzu). Short case series. Dog 1 (Siberian Husky) had prior hemoperitoneum and biopsy-confirmed HCC; dog 2 (Shih Tzu) had persistent liver enzyme elevations and a suspected hepatic tumor. Computed tomography (CT) showed right divisional masses (91.8 × 122.3 × 101.4 mm; 77.0 × 94.8 × 70.2 mm) with CVC compression or involvement and no pre-existing collateral venous return. A percutaneously controlled hydraulic occluder was placed around the pre-renal CVC. Gradual outpatient occlusion was performed over 79 and 44 days while monitoring saphenous venous pressure, renal values, and hindlimb edema. Complete CVC occlusion and collateralization were confirmed by CT before en bloc right divisional hepatectomy with segmental CVC resection. Macroscopically complete resection was achieved in both dogs. Complete HCC resection was confirmed histopathologically. Morbidity was limited to transient wound exudation in dog 1 and transient ascites in dog 2. No recurrence or metastasis was identified in dog 1 during follow-up. In dog 2, no clinical signs suggestive of recurrence or metastasis were reported. Survival after hepatectomy was 352 and 2467 days. Staged pre-renal CVC occlusion may establish collateral venous return and permit planned en bloc right divisional hepatectomy with segmental CVC resection in carefully selected dogs with right divisional HCC involving the CVC.

records.title: Bilateral Third Eyelid Ectopic Cilia in a Maine Coon Cat.
records.abstract: To describe a case of a Maine Coon cat diagnosed with bilateral aberrant hairs consistent with ectopic cilia arising from the third eyelid. The history, clinical signs, examination findings, surgical procedures, and case outcome were reviewed. An eleven-month-old Maine Coon cat presented with a chronic history of bilateral epiphora and right blepharospasm. The left eye previously underwent upper and lower eyelid wedge excision to shorten the palpebral fissure and a partial Celsus-Hotz procedure to correct lower eyelid entropion. The right eye developed lower eyelid entropion shortly after and was surgically treated using the Read and Broun technique. Examination revealed a bilateral ocular discharge and follicular conjunctivitis; macroblepharon, permanent lower eyelid entropion associated with trichiasis, and non-ulcerative keratitis were present in the right eye. The upper and lower eyelid position was normal in the left eye. The right eye was treated with the Stades Diabolo technique and a partial Celsus-Hotz procedure. Inspection under general anesthesia revealed bilateral single aberrant hairs consistent with ectopic cilia on the palpebral surface of the third eyelid. A focal conjunctivectomy, including the ectopic cilium, was performed in each eye. Eyelid and conjunctival wounds healed uneventfully. Differential diagnoses for aberrant hair arising from the third eyelid conjunctiva include dermoid, choristoma, or ectopic cilium. Histology was declined due to financial constraints. Although not previously reported in the literature, given the clinical appearance, an ectopic cilium is the most likely diagnosis. Surgical excision was curative, with no recurrence of epiphora, conjunctivitis, or the entropion.

records.title: Corneal Sequestration and Bilateral Distichiasis in a Binturong (Arctictis binturong).
records.abstract: To report the first documented case of corneal sequestration and distichiasis in a binturong (Arctictis binturong), discuss implications of disease prevalence in a non-domestic feliform, and hypothesize on potential etiology and predisposing factors for corneal sequestration. A 15-year-old intact male binturong. Anesthetized physical examination and ophthalmic assessment were performed by board-certified specialists. Corneal cytology, culture and sensitivity, debridement of the sequestra in lieu of keratectomy, histopathology, and cryoepilation were performed, followed by 4 weeks of topical therapy. The patient was euthanized 3 years later for unrelated reasons, and a necropsy was performed. Examination found bilateral distichiasis. In the left cornea, two brown, ovoid lesions flanked an area of yellow infiltrate, all overlying a raised, ulcerated granulation bed. Corneal cytology identified neutrophils, cocci, and rare rods. Histopathology of the debrided tissue showed coagulative to lytic necrosis with intralesional gram-positive cocci, indicating sequestration and secondary infection. Aerobic culture yielded Staphylococcus delphini and Streptococcus acidominimus. Photo updates 4 weeks post-operation showed resolution of clinical signs. Later, necropsy and histology showed chronic ocular changes without recurrence of sequestra. Clinical and histopathologic findings identified corneal sequestration, with chronic irritation secondary to distichiasis as a suspected factor. Surgical debridement and cryoepilation achieved long-term clinical resolution, with only mild distichiae regrowth and no sequestration recurrence after 3 years. Corneal sequestration is thought to predominantly affect domestic cats (Felis catus); this report expands the clinical relevance of corneal sequestration to an exotic species and supports chronic corneal irritation as a predisposing factor.

records.title: Technical note: Combined approach for total mandibulectomy.
records.abstract: To describe a novel combined approach for total mandibulectomy (CATM) by combining a lateral approach for condylectomy and a ventral approach for total mandibulectomy. Descriptive technical note utilizing a cadaveric study and clinical case. One dog cadaver (27 kg, mixed breed) and one clinical case (2.5-year-old castrated male Australian Shepherd). The CATM technique was evaluated in a dog cadaver prior to clinical application in a dog with a left mandibular soft tissue sarcoma. Condylectomy was performed by a lateral approach to the temporomandibular joint followed by a ventral paramedian approach for left total mandibulectomy. CATM was successfully performed in both the cadaveric model and clinical case without intraoperative complications. Extending the lateral condylectomy incision caudally allowed for regional lymphadenectomy in the clinical case. Medial drift of the right mandible resulted in palatal contact trauma that was successfully managed with crown height reduction and vital pulpotomy. At two months postoperatively, the dog maintained good clinical function without tumor recurrence or additional adverse effects. The CATM was a feasible technique that provided increased TMJ exposure for joint disarticulation and condylectomy. The CATM provides a safe and effective technique for total mandibulectomy that optimizes TMJ access, facilitating joint disarticulation and condylectomy, while enhancing visualization of neurovascular structures.

records.title: Removal of a Posteriorly Luxated Lens Using Pars Plana Vitrectomy and Perfluorocarbon Liquid: A Case Report.
records.abstract: To report a case of canine posterior lens luxation in which the intact lens was successfully floated using perfluorocarbon liquid (PFCL) combined with pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) and subsequently removed. A client-owned 7-year-old castrated female Italian Greyhound presented with rapidly progressive bilateral posterior lens luxation. In the right eye, via a three-port 25-gauge pars plana approach, the vitreous was removed and PFCL was injected beneath the luxated lens to float the intact lens from the retinal surface to the pupillary plane. The lens was subsequently removed by intracapsular lens extraction through a limbal incision using a cryoprobe. At the final 6-month follow-up examination, vision was preserved, and no retinal detachment or other significant postoperative complications were observed. In this case, combining PPV and PFCL was an effective technique for managing posterior lens luxation and enabled successful removal of the intact luxated lens.

records.title: Three-dimensional printed dorsal occipitocervical fixation in a dog with atlantoaxial instability and concurrent incomplete ossification of the atlas.
records.abstract: A 5-year-old, male, neutered, Border Collie presented to a referral hospital with marked cervical hyperaesthesia, uncharacteristic aggression and progressive tetraparesis. The dog was diagnosed with chronic, dynamic atlantoaxial instability and incomplete ossification of the atlas using combined advanced cross-sectional imaging. Traditional surgical approaches rely on adequate bone stock from both the atlas and the axis to achieve robust fixation, which would have been challenging in this case. Descriptive surgical techniques are lacking for this presentation due to its rarity. The owner consented to a novel surgical technique that used a three-dimensional (3D) printed titanium alloy plate to achieve dorsal occipitocervical fixation. A single screw deviated from it's intended corridor in the calvarium by 2.43 mm. The dog demonstrated transient worsening of neurological deficits and regained full ambulation 4 weeks post operative. 3D printing is becoming a popular adjunct in evolving surgical techniques and can be considered in both traditional and rare presentations.

records.title: Corneal stromal metastasis of urothelial carcinoma in a dog.
records.abstract: A 15-year-old intact male Miniature Dachshund presented with severe hematuria. Clinical evaluations of this dog raised the suspicion of a malignant bladder tumor, and corneal stromal opacity was observed in the left eye. Because of the critical condition, the dog died on the day of presentation, after which a necropsy was performed. Necropsy and histopathological examinations confirmed urothelial carcinoma (UC) in the bladder. Moreover, the corneal stromal opacity represented a metastatic lesion of UC, and similar metastatic lesions were identified at 13 other sites. The UC in this dog was considered clinically highly malignant based on its rapid clinical course and the presence of multiple metastatic sites. This highly malignant nature may have contributed to the corneal stromal metastasis. This is an extremely rare case of corneal stromal metastasis from canine UC.

records.title: Feline cutaneous mast cell tumor with extensive macrophage-associated cell-in-cell structures.
records.journal: Journal of veterinary diagnostic investigation : official publication of the American Association of Veterinary Laboratory Diagnosticians, Inc
records.abstract: An 8-y-old, castrated male Korean Shorthair cat was presented to a veterinary clinic for evaluation of a cutaneous mass on the left inner thigh. Microscopic examination revealed a poorly circumscribed dermal neoplasm composed of poorly granulated, pleomorphic neoplastic mast cells with frequent cell-in-cell structures. Notably, viable neoplastic mast cells were engulfed by large macrophages, indicating a specific form of the cell-in-cell phenomenon. Immunohistochemistry for c-KIT, IBA1, and cleaved caspase-3 was used to support the diagnosis. To our knowledge, cell-in-cell phenomenon has not been previously described in feline cutaneous mast cell tumors, nor has the clinical outcome of such cases been reported.
